 Hyderabad Chronicle Swati Sharma 17 Nov 2026 6:30 PM IST 17 Nov 2026 6:30 PM IST Discovered on Instagram rather than through a film-family network, Satvika Veeravalli is making her Telugu debut with one clear ambition: to let her work speak for itself
 x Satvika Veeravalli. (DC) As Preferred
Source Satvika Veeravalli’s route to Telugu cinema runs through engineering, Oracle and a decision to exchange corporate certainty for a profession without guarantees. She makes her debut opposite Dulquer Salmaan in Aakasamlo Oka Tara.
 “Leaving my job at Oracle led to vitriol. People felt leaving a secure job should not be glorified, and that films meant fame, money and visibility. ‘Who wouldn’t choose acting? Is this such a big thing to melodramatise?’ Engineering was a path I chose for myself, and struggled to bring to fruition. I was at a crossroads: a career I had dedicated years to stabilising, or one that breeds instability. It wasn’t easy,” says the 26-year-old.
 Nor does she mistake cinema for an uncomplicated prize. “Film comes with things I would never see in a corporate atmosphere: attacks on my personal character, digging into my background and family, and an irreversible lack of privacy. Fame, money and status are not guaranteed. Those who achieve them are a very small minority,” says an Indian-American actress.
 She had personal savings and supportive parents as a safety net. The story moved her, while three reputed production houses gave her confidence. “When an opportunity of this magnitude comes in search of you, it feels like fate is willing you in a certain direction. I’m glad I made the shift. It’s been incredibly fulfilling.”
 “People assume that we live in a vacuum, completely untethered from our parents’ culture. I find it’s actually the opposite.” Her parents introduced her to Bharatanatyam and Carnatic music. Summer training built her confidence as an artist.
 “As an NRI, and most importantly as someone who does not have a godfather or connections in the industry, I will always work to prove my mettle, that I belong in TFI. I can do my level best in learning the language and craft, but accepting me is ultimately the audience’s prerogative.”
 She is direct about being called an “industry plant. “I have no film background. I was discovered on Instagram by a producer, who now represents me. But all the opportunities I’ve signed, came via extensive auditions.” She recognises the privilege of the launch. The fraternity has welcomed her warmly; Allu Arjun was kind enough to attend the film’s Nov 15 pre-release event.
 “Much of who I am as an actor, at this point, is the result of observing and learning from actors like him on set. It’s an honour to be a heroine in a Dulquer film.”
 Her character’s ambition to achieve something larger than herself struck a chord. Engineering was a struggle. Weak in mathematics and without a background in physics, she battled self-doubt and mental health challenges, which she openly shared online. Determined to graduate early, she completed the programme in three years through intensive coursework, campus work and research. “It was difficult, led to many instances of self-doubt, but let me prove to myself that I had immense capability.”
 Even if Aakasamlo Oka Tara were her last film, she says, she would feel “immense gratitude, pride and joy”. Five years from now, she hopes that feeling persists.
 “I don’t have a body of work that allows me to say no to any role right off the bat. My boundaries are largely circumstantial and subject to my personal comfort and resonance with a storyline.”
